overview:
Ayambil Oli, often called Navpad Oli or simply Oli, is a nine-day Jain observance centred on the Siddhachakra and the Navpad – the nine supreme positions honoured in the Navkar Mantra. It is kept twice a year, in the bright fortnight (shukla paksha) of the lunar months of Chaitra (spring) and Ashwin/Aso (autumn), from the seventh day (Saptami) to the full moon (Purnima). In many communities, especially among Śvetāmbara mūrtipūjaka Jains, the autumn Ayambil Oli is more widely observed because mendicants are often resident near lay communities during the rainy-season retreat.

The core practice of Ayambil Oli is the vow of ayambil tapa: taking only one simple, boiled, bland meal per day, usually in daylight, without oil, ghee, milk, curd, sugar, salt, fruits, green vegetables, or fried items. The food is prepared to minimise taste and sensory stimulation, so that the practitioner can focus on inner restraint (saṃyama), reduction of attachment to flavour (rasaparityāga), and contemplation of the nine pads of the Siddhachakra. This makes Ayambil Oli an example of external austerity (bāhya tapa) that supports internal austerities such as meditation, scriptural study, and reflection on the qualities of the liberated and the spiritually advanced.

The nine days of the festival are mapped to the nine positions of the Siddhachakra: the five Panch Parameṣṭhi (Arihant, Siddha, Ācārya, Upādhyāya, Sādhu) and the four spiritual qualities or supports (Darśana – right faith, Jñāna – right knowledge, Cāritra – right conduct, and Tapas – austerity). Each day is devoted to one pad, with sermons, pūjā, stavan (hymns), and meditation structured around its meaning. For example, the first day honours the Arihant, the embodied omniscient teacher free from attachment and aversion; the second honours the Siddha, the disembodied liberated soul; subsequent days focus on the heads of the order, teachers of scripture, ascetics, and the three jewels (ratnatraya) plus austerity. In many sanghs, the colour, grain, and iconography used in worship on each day symbolically correspond to the pad being venerated.

Ayambil Oli is closely linked with the worship of the Siddhachakra yantra and the narrative of Śrīpāḷ and Mayṇāsundarī. Traditional accounts describe King Śrīpāḷ, afflicted with leprosy, and his devoted wife Mayṇāsundarī, who, under the guidance of the monk Munichandra, performs Navpad Oli with Siddhachakra Mahāpūjā and ayambil fasting for nine days. Through her steadfast observance, Śrīpāḷ and many other sufferers are cured, and the couple attains prosperity and spiritual progress. This story is used in sermons to illustrate the power of right faith, disciplined austerity, and compassionate support within marriage, rather than as a literal medical prescription.

Socially, Ayambil Oli has become strongly associated with married women in many Śvetāmbara communities, who often take the lead in organising the festival, preparing ayambil food, and attending daily discourses. The observance is believed to foster harmony in married life, the well-being of the family, and protection from certain ailments, especially skin diseases, when undertaken with right intention and ethical conduct. At the same time, men, youth, and elders also participate, and the theological focus of the festival is universal: veneration of the Navpad and cultivation of the three jewels of Jainism.

From a doctrinal perspective, Ayambil Oli is not a scripturally mandated compulsory fast for all Jains but a widely accepted traditional observance (śāśvata atthai in some lists of eternal fasts) that integrates lay austerity with devotion to the Siddhachakra. It is framed as a means to reduce passions (kṣaya of krodha, māna, lobha, māyā), accumulate meritorious karma (puṇya) through worship and charity, and prepare the mind for deeper practices such as pratikramaṇa and svādhyāya. Contemporary teachers often emphasise that the true fruit of Ayambil Oli lies in inner transformation—gentleness, non-violence, honesty, and detachment—rather than in external ritual alone.

Because Ayambil Oli involves dietary restriction and fasting, responsible practice requires attention to health, age, and medical conditions. Traditional texts and modern teachers alike advise that children, pregnant persons, the elderly, and those with illnesses such as diabetes or eating disorders should only undertake ayambil under medical guidance and with the counsel of qualified Jain teachers, adapting the observance when necessary. The ethical heart of Jainism is non-harm (ahiṃsā), which includes avoiding harm to one’s own body and mind; therefore, any austerity, including Ayambil Oli, must be balanced with care, consent, and informed judgment.

primary_sources.title: Navakāra Mantra (Namokāra Mantra)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the omniscient Tirthankaras; canonical usage in Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions
primary_sources.original_text:
णमो अरिहंताणं
णमो सिद्धाणं
णमो आयरियाणं
णमो उवज्झायाणं
णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṇamo arihaṃtāṇaṃ
ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ
ṇamo āyariyāṇaṃ
ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ
ṇamo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ
primary_sources.translation:
Obeisance to the Arihants.
Obeisance to the Siddhas.
Obeisance to the Ācāryas.
Obeisance to the Upādhyāyas.
Obeisance to all Sādhus in the world.
primary_sources.notes: This mantra, preserved in Prakrit across both major Jain traditions, is the doctrinal foundation of the Navpad and the Siddhachakra. Ayambil Oli is explicitly oriented around these five Parameṣṭhis plus four additional pads (right faith, right knowledge, right conduct, and austerity). The mantra itself does not prescribe Ayambil Oli, but later ritual manuals and commentaries connect the nine-day observance to the nine positions implied by the mantra and its expansions.

primary_sources.title: Siddhachakra-stavana and Navapada-stotra (various ritual manuals)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous or sectarian ritual compilers; often attributed within lineages to ācāryas such as Ācārya Haribhadra or later authors, though attribution varies
primary_sources.original_text:
अरिहंताणं नमो, सिद्धाणं नमो,
आयरियाणं नमो, उवज्झायाणं नमो,
सव्वसाहूणं नमो, सद्धम्मस्स नमो,
सम्यग्दसणस्स नमो, सम्यग्ज्ञानस्स नमो,
सम्यक्चरित्तस्स नमो, तपस्स नमो।
primary_sources.transliteration:
arihantāṇaṃ namo, siddhāṇaṃ namo,
āyariyāṇaṃ namo, uvajjhāyāṇaṃ namo,
savvasāhūṇaṃ namo, saddhammasa namo,
samyag-dasaṇassa namo, samyag-ñāṇassa namo,
samyak-carittassa namo, tapassa namo.
primary_sources.translation:
Homage to the Arihants, homage to the Siddhas,
Homage to the Ācāryas, homage to the Upādhyāyas,
Homage to all Sādhus, homage to the true Dharma,
Homage to right faith, homage to right knowledge,
Homage to right conduct, homage to austerity.
primary_sources.notes: This type of hymn, in Prakrit or mixed Sanskrit-Prakrit, is recited during Siddhachakra worship and Navpad Oli. It explicitly lists the nine pads that structure Ayambil Oli. The exact wording varies across manuscripts and sectarian prayer books, and the above text represents a commonly printed form rather than a single critical edition. Ritual manuals then prescribe nine days of ayambil fasting, daily pūjā of the Siddhachakra, and sermons on each pad.

primary_sources.title: Śrīpāḷ-Mayṇāsundarī narrative (Śrīpāḷ-rāsa / Śrīpāḷ-caritra)
primary_sources.author: Later Jain poets; versions exist in Apabhraṃśa, Old Gujarati, and other vernaculars, with varying attributions
primary_sources.original_text:
… Munichandra-munīe teṇaṃ Navapadaṇiṃ Oliṃ kahī,
Siddhacakka-mahāpujāeṃ, ayambila-tavaṃ karihi.
Mayṇāsundarīe bhattīeṇaṃ, niyamaṇiṃ dhāraī,
Śrīpāḷa-lepra-rogāeṃ, kṣaṇa-māeṃ nivāraī …
primary_sources.transliteration:
… Munichandra-munīe teṇaṃ navapadaṇiṃ oliṃ kahī,
siddhacakka-mahāpujāeṃ, ayambila-tavaṃ karihi.
mayṇāsundarīe bhattīeṇaṃ, niyamaṇiṃ dhāraī,
śrīpāḷa-lepra-rogāeṃ, kṣaṇa-māeṃ nivāraī …
primary_sources.translation:
… The monk Munichandra instructed them in the Navpad Oli,
"Perform the great worship of the Siddhachakra and undertake the ayambil austerity."
With devoted faith, Mayṇāsundarī upheld the discipline,
And in a moment she dispelled Śrīpāḷ’s disease of leprosy …
primary_sources.notes: This excerpt represents the style and content of vernacular narrative texts used in sermons about Ayambil Oli; exact wording differs between editions. The story situates Ayambil Oli and Siddhachakra Mahāpūjā in a mythic past (often linked to the era of the twentieth Tirthankara, Munisuvrata). It is a Tier B–C source: a traditional narrative rather than canonical āgama. Teachers use it to illustrate the spiritual efficacy of disciplined fasting and worship, but modern guidance stresses that it should not be taken as a substitute for medical treatment.

misconceptions.myth: Ayambil Oli is a compulsory fast that every Jain must observe, regardless of age or health.
misconceptions.reality: Ayambil Oli is a revered but optional traditional observance. Jain doctrine places ahiṃsā, including non-harm to oneself, above rigid austerity. Children, pregnant persons, the elderly, and those with medical conditions are encouraged to adapt or refrain from ayambil under medical advice and the guidance of qualified teachers, rather than feeling coerced to participate.

misconceptions.myth: Ayambil Oli is only for married women and has no relevance for men, youth, or ascetics.
misconceptions.reality: While Ayambil Oli is socially associated with married women in many Śvetāmbara communities, its theological focus—the Navpad and Siddhachakra—is universal. Men, youth, and ascetics also observe ayambil and participate in Siddhachakra worship. The festival’s core aims are spiritual: cultivating right faith, knowledge, conduct, and austerity for all practitioners.

misconceptions.myth: Observing Ayambil Oli guarantees miraculous cures for diseases, especially skin conditions.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional stories like that of Śrīpāḷ and Mayṇāsundarī describe dramatic healings to highlight the power of faith and discipline, but they are not medical prescriptions. Contemporary Jain teachers emphasise that Ayambil Oli is a spiritual practice that may support mental clarity and ethical living, not a guaranteed cure. Responsible practice includes seeking appropriate medical care and not using fasting as a replacement for treatment.

misconceptions.myth: The main purpose of Ayambil Oli is physical detox or weight loss.
misconceptions.reality: Ayambil Oli is framed in Jain tradition as an austerity aimed at reducing attachment to taste, weakening passions, and deepening devotion to the Navpad. Any physical effects are secondary. Treating Ayambil primarily as a diet or detox undermines its ethical and spiritual intent and can lead to unhealthy attitudes toward food and the body.

misconceptions.myth: Only the external rules of food (no oil, no spices, one meal) matter; inner attitude is irrelevant.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts and teachers consistently stress that external austerities are meaningful only when accompanied by inner transformation—humility, non-violence, honesty, and detachment. During Ayambil Oli, practitioners are encouraged to avoid anger, pride, greed, and deceit, to engage in svādhyāya and pratikramaṇa, and to cultivate compassion. Without this inner work, the fast is considered incomplete.
